title: AegisBid Omega
subtitle: Fault-Tolerant, Verifiable and Disaster-Recoverable Flash Auctions

blocks.text: Abstract. AegisBid Omega separates durable bid admission, transactional decision authority, realtime presentation, independently verifiable evidence and disaster recovery. PostgreSQL serializes auction decisions; NATS JetStream journals commands; a Go gateway coalesces authoritative snapshots for large subscriber sets. Next.js exposes bidder, seller, administrator and auditor views. Bacula, physical WAL recovery and an encrypted remote S3 repository address distinct recovery failures. Evidence includes a 50,000-socket hold, database-primary failover, physical PITR and an actual AWS backup/restore. Deployment templates exist for three-zone Kubernetes; a real EKS deployment was not executed.
1.1 Problem definition and correctness contract

Flash auctions combine a hot ordering key, a deadline, limited stock and retry-prone clients. A fast HTTP response or WebSocket broadcast cannot establish acceptance. The system distinguishes QUEUED admission from committed ACCEPTED / REJECTED / CLOSED outcomes. One globally unique request UUID binds an immutable auction, authenticated bidder and integer-cent amount. Same-payload retries reuse the record; changed payloads conflict. Final allocation contains at most stock distinct bidders. Payment processing, fulfillment and tax settlement are outside the implementation.

blocks.text: 1.2 Authority boundaries and actual data movement

The SQL intake journal closes the database-to-broker publication gap. Admission commits a request before returning QUEUED; a relay subsequently publishes it with Nats-Msg-Id=request_id. Consequently, QUEUED proves durable SQL intake, not a JetStream quorum acknowledgment. Workers reconcile SQL pending rows independently of notifications. The outbox publishes live subjects, but the implemented Go gateway currently polls the authenticated snapshot API rather than consuming those subjects. Redis is not required and is not the decision authority.

This separation permits disconnected clients to resolve old UUIDs, prevents notification loss from reversing decisions, and supports recovery when PostgreSQL and NATS snapshots are not simultaneous. It also exposes the main trade-off: a hot auction is deliberately serialized, while snapshot distribution and different auctions can scale separately. Source: aegis/api.py, engine.py, pipeline.py; services/realtime/gateway/main.go.

Restores use isolated targets and do not automatically cut over production traffic.

blocks.text: 2.2 Bid decision transaction

Auction locks are acquired before lease locks, giving one transactionally ordered authority per auction [1]. Every decision uses the currently acquired epoch; a competing live lease or stale expected epoch raises Fenced. An expired lease can be reacquired with an incremented epoch. A crash before commit rolls back changes. A crash after commit but before broker acknowledgment can cause redelivery; the existing non-QUEUED SQL request and unique decision key prevent a second business effect. This is at-least-once delivery with idempotent effects, not exactly-once network transport [2].
2.3 Price, deadline and allocation semantics

required = max(min_price_cents, high + increment_cents)
           when a high offer exists; otherwise min_price_cents
eligible admission interval = [opens_at, closes_at)
winners = first stock of distinct current offers
          ordered by amount DESC, decision_seq ASC

The rule is a strict global increment: two equal-price offers cannot both advance the high offer. A bidder may replace an offer with a larger eligible amount. Monetary values use BIGINT cents, avoiding floating-point rounding. Eligibility uses the database-stamped admission time, not browser click time or eventual processing time. Closing locks the auction, verifies that the deadline is due, drains pending requests, materializes ranked winners and appends the close event atomically. Administrative close moves the deadline under the same auction lock.

The database enforces identity/sequence uniqueness; the transaction implements ranking, stock bounds and price rules. SQL privileges are not a WORM ledger: an administrator can alter tables, so independent trusted anchors/signatures remain essential. Static review also identifies a lifecycle edge: intake currently permits requests against an already CLOSED auction while background reconciliation scans OPEN auctions. Such requests can remain QUEUED; a production admission guard or closed-request reconciliation is still required. Source: infra/postgres/001_core.sql; aegis/engine.py, rules.py, pipeline.py.

pages.title: Realtime scaling, API contracts and user workflows

blocks.text: 3.1 Bounded realtime fanout

The Go gateway authenticates the session through /v1/auth/me, caching token-hash-to-subject results for up to 30 seconds. A per-auction hub obtains one authoritative snapshot per second and shares a prepared WebSocket frame across subscribers [3]. Each client has one pending update slot: newer snapshots replace stale queued updates. Readers enforce a 1,024-byte input limit, a 60-second read deadline and pong renewal; writers use a five-second deadline and 20-second pings. Three consecutive snapshot-source failures close subscribers to force reconciliation. The gateway never decides a bid.

Default gateway limits are 60,000 total/per-auction connections and ten connections per user, scoped to one process. The production renderer caps each gateway at 25,000 connections and supplies three replicas plus CPU autoscaling to twelve replicas. The 50k experiment explicitly raised the demo user's quota. DB pools bound each process/DSN to 1..16 connections, with five-second acquisition/connect timeouts; these are not general SQL statement deadlines. Admission rejects a per-auction queue above 10,000 records. API bidding and login limits are also process-local, not fleet-wide quotas.

blocks.text: 3.2 Four operational roles

Bidder: auction cards, stock, high/required offer, countdown, integer-cent entry, queued/final state, history and winners. Pending UUIDs survive uncertain responses in local storage. Seller: configure and schedule auctions, preview the active view and end owned auctions. Administrator: decision counts, rates, latency quantiles, queue/outbox depth, leader epochs, backup/restore state and the chaos switchboard. Auditor: load/download sanitized ledger evidence for independent CLI verification. These are shared-codebase role views; server authorization, not hidden buttons, controls access.

Clients reconnect, refresh snapshots and discard older versions. The UI is an eventually refreshed projection, not a linearizable price oracle; final outcomes come from request lookup. Admin socket telemetry from the API is process-specific; Go counts are exposed separately and require full replica discovery/aggregation for fleet totals. Source: apps/web/app/page.js; aegis/api.py; scripts/render_ha.py.
4.1 Identity, privilege and transport boundaries

Passwords use salted scrypt (N=16,384; r=8; p=1). HS256 session tokens carry subject, issuer aegisbid and a four-hour expiry; decoding requires issuer/expiry/subject and a sufficiently long secret. Cookies are HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict and Secure in production. Bidder identity is loaded server-side; bid schemas forbid extra identity fields and reject fractional cents. Owner checks protect private request history and receipts. Explicit PUBLIC_ORIGIN checks handle TLS proxies; the Go upgrader also validates origins. Per-process rate/connection limits and bounded queues constrain overload.

Production manifests add PostgreSQL CA verification, TLS NATS clients and mutually validated NATS routes, read-only application filesystems, dropped capabilities, disabled automatic service-account token mounts, secure bootstrap secrets and default-deny network policies. API pods do not receive S3 backup credentials. Database and backup keys remain outside browser code. The current authentication is a prototype identity system, not a complete public-service IAM/MFA, account lifecycle or fleet-wide abuse-management solution.
4.2 Black-box ledger and BidDNA evidence

H_0 = 64 zero characters
H_i = SHA256(ASCII(H_(i-1)) || canonical_JSON(event_i))
canonical_JSON: sorted keys, compact separators, ASCII escaping
bidder pseudonym = SHA256(string UUID)
manifest signature = Ed25519(canonical unsigned manifest)

Events include request identity, pseudonymous bidder, amount, admission time, outcome, intake order and decision sequence. The export fixes schema version, auction rules, ordered events, final winners and terminal anchor under a repeatable-read SQL snapshot. Signing occurs only when AUDIT_SIGNING_KEY is configured. A receipt is a private event/hash reference; it is not a separate payment credential or independent signature. UUID pseudonyms hide raw bidder IDs in exports but do not prevent the operator from retaining the identity mapping.

The verifier deliberately does not import the engine's rule evaluator. It rechecks contiguous event order, predecessor/digest links, duplicate requests, admission cutoff, price progression, distinct offers, allocation order, stock bounds, close placement, exported version and stored winners. Ed25519 verification requires an independently trusted public key. Changed, missing or reordered evidence fails. Unsigned evidence reports INCOMPLETE rather than trusted PASS. A signed chain detects changes relative to its anchor; it cannot prove honesty of the original signer.

pages.title: High availability, backup and disaster recovery

blocks.text: 5.1 Replicated authority and zone placement

CloudNativePG 1.30.1 manages three PostgreSQL instances with ANY 1 synchronous standby acknowledgment, required durability, failover quorum and isolation liveness checks. The operator controls promotion and the read/write service; application leases cannot fence two independently writable PostgreSQL primaries. Three operator replicas protect coordination. PostgreSQL and NATS have required zone anti-affinity; stateless pods spread and can rebalance over two healthy zones. Gateway HPA uses a 60% CPU target and 600-second scale-down stabilization. Insufficient safe database/broker quorum must preserve consistency rather than invent success [6].

The validated EKS template provisions three public/private subnet pairs, independent NAT egress per zone, private managed workers, encrypted disks, Kubernetes-secret KMS protection, explicit administrator access, audit logs and EBS CSI Pod Identity. Ingress/TLS and published image digests remain commissioning inputs. The real test stopped one kind worker, verified it was no longer running, observed standby promotion, compared the ledger, retried prior UUIDs and rejected a stale worker epoch. Those container-node labels are not physical AWS zones.

blocks.text: 5.2 Offsite protection and recovery coverage

The real AWS test used a private Singapore repository with public-access blocking, client encryption, server-side AES256 and 30-day COMPLIANCE retention. It uploaded prepared artifacts, verified retention/version metadata, observed deletion denial, downloaded exact versions, authenticated/decrypted files and restored an isolated database. Decryption keys/receipts were preserved outside the repository and application containers. This is actual remote storage, but it uses the configured account rather than a separately administered backup account. The local S3-compatible drill additionally verified that a corrupt newer index cannot replace the pinned original.

Production continuous remote WAL uses the Barman Cloud plugin 0.16.0, an ObjectStore, a WAL-archiver cluster patch and scheduled physical backups. Bacula Catalog/configuration, timeline history, backup receipts and signing/decryption keys also need independent recovery. A successful upload or job does not establish a usable restore. Report RTO only for the timed interval and RPO only against an explicit failure/checkpoint; the implemented drill timers exclude full site reconstruction. No production promotion or traffic rerouting occurs automatically during sandbox restoration.

blocks.text: 6.1 Interpretation and remaining engineering work

Measurements were collected on Windows 11 with Docker Desktop, Python 3.13, PostgreSQL 18, NATS 2.11, Next.js 16.4.6 and Bacula 9.6.7. The socket generators shared one host and demo identity with an elevated quota: the result does not establish 50,000 unique bidders, simultaneous bids or hot-auction decision throughput. HTTP latency includes the harness's completion polling; it is not raw transaction service time. Recovery figures use small controlled datasets and are not full-site RPO/RTO guarantees. No real whole-zone outage, multi-host 50k benchmark, old-FlashBid-system comparison or payment settlement was demonstrated.

The current AWS principal permits S3 but denies EKS management inventory. Thus multi-zone infrastructure is implemented and validated, not launched in AWS. Further work includes an authorized infrastructure role, independently administered backup account, real-zone exercises, fleet-wide quotas, advance capacity warming and the closed-auction intake edge noted on page 3. Hash chains are tamper-evident relative to trusted evidence, not physically immutable SQL storage. These limits are part of the technical result.
6.2 Reproduction, delivery and references

Source baseline: commit 6a0d253. Eight implementation phases used phase branches, local checks, pushes and no-fast-forward merges; evidence is in docs/evidence. Core check: set RUN_INTEGRATION=1 and RUN_NATS=1 against disposable services, then pytest -q. Run scripts.socket_capacity, scripts.rehearse_pitr and scripts.rehearse_ha only in their documented environments. Cloud backup scripts create retained objects; use recorded evidence for the three-minute presentation rather than rerunning billable cloud actions. See README.md, docs/production.md and docs/ha-deployment.md.
